summary: An FYI document containing biographical information about members of the IAB, the IESG, and the IRSG. It is informational and gives a picture of the people leading Internet standards at the time.

eli5.summary: A who's who book that tells you a little about the people who led Internet technology groups in 1992.

questions: who is on the iab iesg 1992
what is the who's who in the internet rfc
subtitle: A 1992 collection of self-written biographies from the people serving on the IAB, IESG and IRSG.

tldr.problem: The Internet is run largely by volunteers, and its wider community knew little about the people who led its standards and research groups.
tldr.mechanism: The compiler asked members of the IAB, IESG and IRSG for short biographies and published 24 of them, in alphabetical order and unedited apart from formatting.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational FYI memo that sets no standard, replaces RFC 1251, and records who led these groups in 1992.

today: RFC 1336 is an Informational FYI memo from May 1992 that specifies no standard. It replaces RFC 1251, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records who sat on these groups in 1991 to 1992 and is a historical snapshot of those people.

sections.title: Why Publish Biographies
sections.content:
RFC 1336 is an FYI document that gathers biographies of members of the Internet Activities Board (IAB), the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) and the Internet Research Steering Group (IRSG). It states that it specifies no standard.

The introduction makes a point about people. The Internet's infrastructure is managed largely by volunteers who give up considerable time. Hundreds of people attend the three IETF meetings each year, and the members of these three groups spend extra time organising the meetings and acting as the IETF's interface to other standards bodies and funding institutions. The author argues that without them the IETF, and the Internet, would not be possible.
sections.eli5: Many people helped build the Internet for free in their spare time, and this document says thank you by introducing the leaders.

sections.title: How the Biographies Were Gathered
sections.content:
In mid-February 1991, the compiler emailed the current members of the IAB, IRSG and IESG. His message noted that the ARPANET was 20 years old and that the next IETF meeting, in St. Louis in March, would be the 20th plenary. It asked each member for a biography of three paragraphs: the first the person's bio, the second school affiliation and other interests, and the third an opinion of how the Internet has grown. He planned to limit inclusion to those three groups for now, with a possible wider set later.

The responses are what the RFC compiles. The compiler also thanks Joyce K. Reynolds for her help with the request message.
sections.eli5: The author sent every leader the same three questions: who are you, what else do you like, and how do you think the Internet grew?

sections.title: What the Biographies Contain
sections.content:
The memo includes 24 biographies, from Philip Almquist to Gregory Vaudreuil. They are in alphabetical order and the contents are unedited, with only the formatting changed. Each heading gives the person's role, such as IETF area director, IAB member or IRSG member.

The entries read as personal career histories. Philip Almquist, for example, describes work at Carnegie-Mellon and Stanford, including leading Stanford's deployment of the Domain Name System, and his role in the Router Requirements Working Group. Robert Braden recounts attaching UCLA's IBM 360/91 to the ARPAnet starting in 1970 and writing TCP/IP code for it, and his reflections on the Internet's scaling problems.

Many entries also end with the author's own view of the Internet's growth, so the document mixes personal history with early opinion about where the network was heading.
sections.eli5: Each page is one person's story: where they worked, what they built and what they think about the Internet growing up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The document is a collection of personal biographies and does not define any protocol that could be attacked or secured.
sections.eli5: This is a book about people, not a computer rule, so there is nothing to lock down.
